claim: RecA forms a helical filament on single stranded DNA that searches for a homologous double stranded DNA and catalyzes the exchange of complementary base pairs to form a new heteroduplex during homologous recombination.
source_text: During homologous recombination, RecA forms a helical filament on a single stranded (ss) DNA that searches for a homologous double stranded (ds) DNA and catalyzes the exchange of complementary base pairs to form a new heteroduplex.
evidence_reasoning: This statement draws from established scientific consensus about RecA function in homologous recombination.

claim: A RecA filament diffuses along a dsDNA track according to the sliding model.
source_text: We present evidence in support of the 'sliding model' wherein a RecA filament diffuses along a dsDNA track.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including FRET measurements and cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Homology can be detected during sliding of the RecA filament.
source_text: We further show that homology can be detected during sliding.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing discrete FRET states corresponding to homology recognition at specific sites during sliding.

claim: Sliding occurs with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 8000 bp²/s.
source_text: Sliding occurs with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 8000 bp 2 /s allowing the filament to sample several hundred base pairs before dissociation.
evidence_reasoning: This value is derived from experimental measurements and Monte Carlo simulations calibrated against cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The RecA filament can sample several hundred base pairs before dissociation.
source_text: Sliding occurs with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 8000 bp 2 /s allowing the filament to sample several hundred base pairs before dissociation.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the measured diffusion coefficient and observed dissociation times ranging from 0.5 to 10 seconds.

claim: Sliding can accelerate homology search by as much as 200 fold.
source_text: Modeling suggests that sliding can accelerate homology search by as much as 200 fold.
evidence_reasoning: This is based on modeling calculations using the measured diffusion coefficient and estimated binding probabilities.

claim: Homology recognition can occur for as few as 6 nt of complementary basepairs.
source_text: Homology recognition can occur for as few as 6 nt of complementary basepairs with the recognition efficiency increasing for higher complementarity.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated experimentally by observing discrete FRET states with 6 nt homology sequences but not with 5 nt sequences.

claim: Recognition efficiency increases for higher complementarity.
source_text: Homology recognition can occur for as few as 6 nt of complementary basepairs with the recognition efficiency increasing for higher complementarity.
evidence_reasoning: Experimental data shows that recognition efficiency increases from ~55% for 6 nt to ~77% for 7 nt homology.

claim: This is the first example of a DNA bound multi-protein complex which can slide along another DNA to facilitate target search.
source_text: Our data represents the first example of a DNA bound multi-protein complex which can slide along another DNA to facilitate target search.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is based on the experimental data presented and comparison with existing literature on protein sliding mechanisms.

claim: Homologous recombination is one of the pathways involved in double strand break repair.
source_text: Homologous recombination is one of the pathways involved in double strand break repair
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Cox et al., 2000) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: RecA homologs Rad51 and Dmc1 in eukaryotes and RadA in archaea carry out similar functions during DNA repair.
source_text: Homologs of RecA, Rad51 and Dmc1 in eukaryotes and RadA in archaea, carry out similar functions during DNA repair underscoring the central role of proteins catalyzing strand exchange across all forms of life
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Bianco et al., 1998) and represents established scientific knowledge about RecA homologs.

claim: Pre-synapsis involves the assembly of RecA monomers on single stranded DNA in the presence of ATP with a stoichiometry of 3 nt per monomer.
source_text: Pre-synapsis involves the assembly of RecA monomers on single stranded (ss) DNA in the presence of ATP with a stoichiometry of 3 nt per monomer
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations (Di Capua et al., 1982; Dombroski et al., 1983) and represents established knowledge about RecA assembly.

claim: RecA forms a filament which stretches the ssDNA to a length of 1.5 times the length of B-form DNA.
source_text: RecA forms a filament which stretches the ssDNA to a length of 1.5 times the length of B-form DNA
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations (Stasiak et al., 1981; Dunn et al., 1982; Stasiak and Egelman, 1986) and represents established structural knowledge.

claim: A RecA filament has to rapidly and accurately find a homologous sequence in the presence of a vast excess of non-homologous dsDNA.
source_text: A RecA filament has to rapidly and accurately find a homologous sequence in the presence of a vast excess of non-homologous dsDNA.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the biological challenge faced during homology search, based on understanding of cellular conditions.

claim: The multivalent nature of the RecA filament enables it to sustain contact with a long dsDNA while allowing for frequent dissociation events that permits rapid sampling of different segments of the DNA.
source_text: The multivalent nature of the RecA filament enables it to sustain contact with a long dsDNA while allowing for frequent dissociation events that permits rapid sampling of different segments of the DNA, thus facilitating homology search
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012) and represents an inference about how multivalency facilitates search.

claim: Random 3D collision between a RecA filament and the dsDNA even when aided by intersegmental transfer is unlikely to result in precise alignment of matching sequences.
source_text: However, random 3D collision between a RecA filament and the dsDNA even when aided by intersegmental transfer is unlikely to result in precise alignment of matching sequences.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the limitations of 3D collision-based search mechanisms.

claim: RecA filament sliding on dsDNA over a short distance range of ten to hundreds of bp would significantly accelerate the search for homology.
source_text: For this reason, RecA filament sliding on dsDNA, even over a short distance range of ten to hundreds of bp would significantly accelerate the search for homology.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the potential benefit of sliding, later supported by experimental data and modeling.

claim: An early study ruled out a role for long range (approximately several kb) 1D sliding during homology search.
source_text: in fact an early study ruled out a role for long range (approximately several kb) 1D sliding during homology search (Adzuma, 1998)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation to Adzuma, 1998.

claim: For short (<80 bp) homologous dsDNA substrates, homology search is completed rapidly (within 30 ms) once the dsDNA encounters a RecA filament.
source_text: For short (<80 bp) homologous dsDNA substrates, homology search is completed rapidly (within 30 ms) once the dsDNA encounters a RecA filament
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Ragunathan et al., 2011) and represents prior experimental findings.

claim: Large and rapid fluctuations in FRET were observed upon docking of non-homologous dsDNA to the RecA filament.
source_text: After docking, we observed large and rapid fluctuations in FRET detected as anti-correlated changes of donor and acceptor intensities.
evidence_reasoning: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The FRET fluctuations are indicative of extensive distance changes between the donor on the dsDNA and the acceptor on the RecA/ssDNA filament.
source_text: The FRET fluctuations are indicative of extensive distance changes between the donor on the dsDNA and the acceptor on the RecA/ssDNA filament.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the observed anti-correlated changes in donor and acceptor intensities, which is the basis of FRET measurements.

claim: The lifetime of the binding events is exponentially distributed with an average lifetime of 3.5 s.
source_text: The lifetime of the binding events is exponentially distributed with an average lifetime of 3.5 s
evidence_reasoning: This is determined from experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Filaments formed with ATP displayed similar FRET fluctuations upon docking of non-homologous dsDNA and exhibit comparable dissociation times.
source_text: Filaments formed with ATP displayed similar FRET fluctuations upon docking of non-homologous dsDNA and exhibit comparable dissociation times
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The fluctuations observed do not require ATP hydrolysis.
source_text: Hence, the fluctuations observed here do not require ATP hydrolysis.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the observation that similar fluctuations occur with both ATP and ATPγS (non-hydrolyzable analog).

claim: Using different lengths for the ssDNA tail (Lfilament = 50 or 99 nt) did not significantly change the lifetime of the encounter complex.
source_text: Using different lengths for the ssDNA tail (Lfilament = 50 or 99 nt) did not significantly change the lifetime of the encounter complex
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Increasing dsDNA length increased the lifetime presumably due to a larger number of contacts between the dsDNA and the RecA filament.
source_text: In contrast, increasing dsDNA length increased the lifetime presumably due to a larger number of contacts between the dsDNA and the RecA filament
evidence_reasoning: The increased lifetime is observed experimentally (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and the explanation is inferred based on structural considerations.

claim: The lifetime of the complex decreased with increasing magnesium or sodium concentrations suggesting that the interaction is electrostatic in nature.
source_text: Rapid FRET fluctuations persisted under all the solution conditions tested while the lifetime of the complex decreased with increasing magnesium or sodium concentrations suggesting that the interaction is electrostatic in nature and can be weakened by increased screening
evidence_reasoning: The decrease in lifetime with increasing salt concentration is observed experimentally (Figure 1D–F), and the electrostatic nature is inferred from this salt dependence.

claim: Eliminating negative charge from the RecA C-terminus by deletion of acidic residues resulted in an increased lifetime of dsDNA bound to the RecA filament.
source_text: Indeed, eliminating negative charge from the RecA C-terminus (Lusetti et al., 2003) by deletion of acidic residues resulted in an increased lifetime of dsDNA bound to the RecA filament
evidence_reasoning: This is observed experimentally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and the C-terminal deletion is based on prior work (Lusetti et al., 2003).

claim: Separation of the duplex ends is not the source of FRET fluctuations.
source_text: When the dsDNA docks to an unlabeled RecA filament immobilized on the surface, we observed stable high FRET (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that separation of the duplex ends is not the source of FRET fluctuations described in Figure 1.
evidence_reasoning: The stable high FRET observed in the control experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) rules out duplex end separation as the cause of fluctuations.

claim: Shorter RecA filaments exhibited faster FRET fluctuations compared to longer filaments.
source_text: Shorter RecA filaments (Lfilament = 21 nt) exhibited faster FRET fluctuations compared to longer filaments (Lfilament = 99 nt)
evidence_reasoning: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The average cross correlation time increased linearly with filament length.
source_text: The average cross correlation time, <τ>, increased linearly with filament length
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in Figure 2C with experimental data points and linear fit.

claim: The linear dependence of cross correlation time on filament length is consistent with 1D diffusion of the RecA filament along dsDNA.
source_text: The average cross correlation time, <τ>, increased linearly with filament length
evidence_reasoning: The linear relationship is expected for 1D diffusion, as confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Monte Carlo simulations with a diffusion coefficient of 0.9 × 10⁻³ μm²/s best fit the experimental data.
source_text: Monte Carlo simulations with a diffusion coefficient of 0.9 × 10⁻³ μm²/s best fit the experimental data
evidence_reasoning: This is determined by comparing experimental data with simulations at different diffusion coefficients (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: The cross correlation time is independent of changes in sodium and magnesium concentrations.
source_text: The cross correlation time is independent of changes in sodium and magnesium concentrations
evidence_reasoning: This is shown experimentally in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The cross correlation time is independent of the co-factor used (ATP or ATPγS).
source_text: The cross correlation time is independent of the co-factor used (ATP or ATPγS)
evidence_reasoning: This is shown experimentally in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Three-color FRET measurements showed anticorrelated emissions between Cy5 and Cy7 acceptors upon docking of Cy3-labeled dsDNA.
source_text: Upon docking of the dsDNA, we observed anticorrelated emissions between the two acceptors (Cy5 and Cy7) as expected for 1D sliding
evidence_reasoning: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The normalized cross correlation plot of ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 showed a negative correlation with a time constant similar to that obtained from two-color experiments.
source_text: The normalized cross correlation plot of ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 showed a negative correlation with a time constant similar to that obtained from two-color experiments
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in Figure 3C with the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The scatter plot of ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 showed unique high FRET regions along both axes, indicating that the dsDNA can reach both acceptor positions.
source_text: The scatter plot of ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 showed unique high FRET regions along both axes (Figure 3D), indicating that the dsDNA can reach both acceptor positions
evidence_reasoning: The scatter plot (Figure 3D) shows the data, and the interpretation about reaching both positions is inferred from the FRET patterns.

claim: The three-color FRET results provide strong support for the 1D sliding model.
source_text: Taken together, the three-color FRET results provide strong support for the 1D sliding model
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the three-color FRET experimental data showing anticorrelated emissions.

claim: For 5 nt homology length, binding of dsDNA to the RecA filament displayed rapid FRET fluctuations across a broad range of FRET values similar to non-homologous sequences.
source_text: Binding of the dsDNA to the RecA filament formed on the ssDNA with the two 5 nt repeats displayed rapid FRET fluctuations across a broad range of FRET values (Figure 4B,E) similar to that observed using a poly-T DNA sequence
evidence_reasoning: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4B,E.

claim: When homology length was increased to 6 nt, single molecule time traces displayed transitions between discrete FRET states.
source_text: In contrast, when we increased the length of homology at HS1 and HS2 by a single nucleotide to Lh = 6 nt, single molecule time traces displayed transitions between discrete FRET states
evidence_reasoning: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The FRET histograms for 6 and 7 nt homology lengths showed distinct FRET peaks.
source_text: The resulting FRET histograms for 6 and 7 nt homology lengths showed distinct FRET peaks (Figure 4F,G)
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 4F,G.

claim: The highest FRET state (approximately 0.9) corresponds to homology recognition and base pairing at HS1.
source_text: Thus, we assigned the highest FRET state (approximately 0.9) to homology recognition and base pairing at HS1
evidence_reasoning: This assignment is based on control experiments with single homology sites (Figure 4H,I).

claim: The mid FRET state (approximately 0.5) corresponds to homology recognition and base pairing at HS2.
source_text: and the mid FRET state (approximately 0.5) to homology recognition and base pairing at HS2
evidence_reasoning: This assignment is based on control experiments with single homology sites (Figure 4H,I).

claim: The lowest FRET state (E ∼ 0.1) corresponds to dsDNA sliding outside the boundary of HS1 and HS2 in a FRET insensitive regime.
source_text: The lowest FRET state, E ∼ 0.1, is likely to correspond to dsDNA sliding outside the boundary of HS1 and HS2 in a FRET insensitive regime.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the FRET value and the lack of stable base pairing at this position.

claim: The rate of departing HS1 or HS2 was threefold lower than that of leaving NH for 6 bp homology.
source_text: The rate of departing HS1 or HS2 was threefold lower than that of leaving NH, showing that even 6 bp homology can significantly stabilize joint molecule formation
evidence_reasoning: This is determined from HMM analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: A slower rate of leaving HS1 and HS2 was observed for Lh = 7 nt compared to Lh = 6 nt.
source_text: As expected, we observed a slower rate of leaving HS1 and HS2 for Lh = 7 nt compared to Lh = 6 nt
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 4L.

claim: The dissociation rate of dsDNA bound to HS1 was higher than that of dsDNA bound to HS2.
source_text: Also, the dissociation rate of dsDNA bound to HS1 was higher than that of dsDNA bound to HS2 possibly because HS1 is located at the filament end
evidence_reasoning: The higher dissociation rate is observed in the data (Figure 4L), and the explanation is inferred based on the position of HS1 at the filament end.

claim: For 6 nt homology, the efficiency of homology site recognition (ErecognitionNH->HS2) is approximately 55%.
source_text: For 6 nt homology (Lh = 6 nt) the efficiency of homology site recognition, ErecognitionNH->HS2 is approximately 55%.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated from the number of transitions observed in the experimental data.

claim: For 7 nt homology, the efficiency of homology site recognition increased to approximately 77%.
source_text: This efficiency increased for 7 nt homology (ErecognitionNH->HS2 for Lh = 7 nt is approximately 77%).
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated from the number of transitions observed in the experimental data.

claim: The efficiency of homology recognition by the RecA filament increases with the number of homologous nucleotides available for basepairing.
source_text: Cumulatively, our data suggest that the efficiency of homology recognition by the RecA filament increases with the number of homologous nucleotides available for basepairing.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the observed increase in recognition efficiency from 55% (6 nt) to 77% (7 nt).

claim: The diffusion constant for RecA filament sliding is approximately 0.9 × 10⁻³ μm²/s or 7700 bp²/s.
source_text: We estimated the diffusion constant, Dslide, for RecA filament sliding to be approximately 0.9 × 10−3 μm2/s or 7700 bp2/s.
evidence_reasoning: This is estimated from cross-correlation analysis and Monte Carlo simulations calibrated against experimental data.

claim: dsDNA would diffuse over a length of 60–300 bp during each encounter with a RecA filament prior to its dissociation.
source_text: Because the lifetime of heterologous synapses ranges from 0.5 to 10 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Mani et al., 2009; Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012), we estimate that dsDNA would diffuse over a length of 60–300 bp during each encounter with a RecA filament prior to its dissociation.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated from the measured diffusion coefficient and observed dissociation times, with support from cited literature.

claim: Even for a recognition probability as low as approximately 1%, sliding leads to a rate enhancement in homology search by approximately 200-fold.
source_text: Though, we do not know the exact microscopic rate constants which determine the binding probability of the RecA filament to the target site (pbind), we can estimate that even for a recognition probability as low as approximately 1%, sliding leads to a rate enhancement in homology search by approximately 200-fold.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated from a theoretical model (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) with estimated parameters.

claim: 1D sliding combined with intersegmental transfer can dramatically accelerate homology search.
source_text: Therefore, 1D sliding combined with intersegmental transfer proposed by Forget and Kowalcyzkowski (2012) can dramatically accelerate homology search.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the calculated rate enhancement and combined with the mechanism proposed in cited work.

claim: A dsDNA that binds to a RecA filament in the wrong orientation cannot establish the correct orientation required for homology recognition without full dissociation and rebinding.
source_text: Therefore, a dsDNA that binds to a RecA filament in the wrong orientation cannot establish the correct orientation required for homology recognition and basepairing without full dissociation and rebinding.
evidence_reasoning: This is concluded from control experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) that rule out dsDNA flipping.

claim: As few as 6 nt of complementary base pairs are sufficient to act as the unit of homology recognition for RecA mediated homology search.
source_text: Our results showed that as few as 6 nt of complementary base pairs are sufficient to act as the unit of homology recognition for RecA mediated homology search.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by the appearance of discrete FRET states with 6 nt homology but not with 5 nt homology.

claim: Recognition of a homology site is a stochastic process.
source_text: It is noteworthy that recognition of a homology site is a stochastic process
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the observation of probabilistic transitions between homology sites and the calculated recognition efficiencies.

claim: Adding even a single nucleotide to the minimum recognition unit of 6 nt improves recognition efficiency by approximately 1.5-fold.
source_text: Furthermore, we show that adding even a single nucleotide to the minimum recognition unit of 6 nt improves recognition efficiency by approximately 1.5-fold.
evidence_reasoning: This is calculated from the observed recognition efficiencies: 77%/55% ≈ 1.4-fold improvement.

claim: 1D sliding during homology search could help RecA reorganize the initial synaptic complex in cis without the need for full dissociation and rebinding.
source_text: While intersegmental transfer serves to bring non-contiguous segments of dsDNA close to each other, 1D sliding during homology search could help RecA reorganize the initial synaptic complex in cis without the need for a RecA filament to fully dissociate and rebind to a nearby homology site located within a short distance (up to few hundred base pairs).
evidence_reasoning: This is a functional inference based on the observed sliding behavior and its implications for homology search.

claim: Sliding could serve as a mechanism to rapidly scan neighboring sequences for the existence of an optimal seed sequence from which base pair propagation and heteroduplex extension reactions can proceed.
source_text: Given the ability of the RecA filament to slide between nearby homology sites (Figure 4), sliding could serve as a mechanism to rapidly scan neighboring sequences for the existence of an optimal seed sequence from which base pair propagation and heteroduplex extension reactions can proceed.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the observed ability to detect homology during sliding (Figure 4) and its biological implications.

claim: It is likely that sliding might also play a role in homology search mediated by Rad51.
source_text: Because of significant structural and functional similarities between RecA and Rad51 (Conway et al., 2004), it is likely that sliding might also play a role in homology search mediated by Rad51.
evidence_reasoning: This is speculated based on structural similarities between RecA and Rad51 (cited from Conway et al., 2004) and the observed sliding behavior of RecA.

claim: An earlier report demonstrated sliding of Rad51 oligomers without any clear functional role attributed to the observed sliding activity.
source_text: An earlier report demonstrated sliding of Rad51 oligomers (not a Rad51 filament bound to ssDNA) without any clear functional role attributed to the observed sliding activity (Graneli et al., 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on citation to Graneli et al., 2006.
